definition: a cleverly devised plan, scheme, or device, often artificial
memoryTip: Con-TRIVE-ance: a clever TRICK or device someone contrived.
correctPassage: The rescue hinged on a last-minute contrivance involving spare rope and a pulley.
wrongPassages: Her contrivance was so genuine that no one doubted a word she said.
After weeks of rest, the meadow returned to its natural contrivance.
The judge praised the witness for his honest contrivance under oath.

definition: to share a boundary with; touch along an edge
memoryTip: A-BUTT against: properties that butt up against each other.
correctPassage: Our backyard abuts a quiet creek that floods only in spring.
wrongPassages: Please abut the meeting until everyone has arrived.
His abut manners made the dinner conversation impossible.
Investors expected an abut forecast with exact quarterly numbers.

definition: persisting tirelessly; incapable of being worn out
correctPassage: An indefatigable coach ran drills with the team until dusk every day.
wrongPassages: The indefatigable nap left her too groggy to finish the assignment.
After one easy practice, the squad declared itself fully indefatigable.
His indefatigable attitude meant he quit whenever the work got hard.

definition: written or published under a false name
memoryTip: PSEUDO + name: a fake name on the byline.
correctPassage: The columnist kept a pseudonymous blog to criticize her own industry.
wrongPassages: The choir sounded pseudonymous once the organ drowned every voice.
She filed a pseudonymous tax return listing her real legal name.
Ops hoped to make the outage pseudonymous by posting a public status update.

definition: to gently push; to lightly encourage toward an action
memoryTip: Elbow NUDGE: a light push that steers without force.
correctPassage: A reminder email can nudge students to finish the form before Friday.
wrongPassages: The wrecking ball gave the wall one final nudge and the building collapsed.
A single nudge of the throttle launched the rocket into orbit.
The shoreline looked nudge once weekend boats filled every slip.

definition: to voluntarily give up or stop claiming something
memoryTip: Re-LINQUISH: let go of a claim or hold (think relinquish the crown).
correctPassage: She refused to relinquish the keys until the lease was signed.
wrongPassages: He decided to relinquish the trophy by training harder than ever.
The brief was so relinquish that it ran thirty pages without a point.
Morning light looked relinquish through the narrow atrium skylight.

definition: to confirm or support as true; to give a personal guarantee
memoryTip: VOUCH for a friend: put your word behind their honesty.
correctPassage: Two former supervisors will vouch for his reliability on the job.
wrongPassages: Admin tried to vouch the complaint volume by hiding the contact form.
The icy trail felt vouch without a single handrail in sight.
She hoped to vouch the rumor by refusing to discuss it at all.

definition: providing additional help; serving as a secondary support
memoryTip: AUX jack: the extra, secondary connection that helps out.
correctPassage: Auxiliary nurses covered the night shift when the ward was short-staffed.
wrongPassages: The auxiliary conductor led the entire orchestra while the maestro sat silent.
They called the plan auxiliary because it replaced every other option.
Her auxiliary deposition was the only evidence the jury ever heard.

definition: to lead an attack, campaign, or major effort
memoryTip: Tip of the SPEAR: you go first and lead the charge.
correctPassage: A small committee will spearhead fundraising for the new library wing.
wrongPassages: He agreed to spearhead the project only by sitting silently in the back row.
The idle machine stayed spearhead through a surge that reset every device.
Fans called the ending spearhead for refusing to resolve any plotline.

definition: to draw out a response, fact, or reaction
memoryTip: E-LICIT draws it out—don't confuse with illicit (illegal).
correctPassage: The interviewer's silence helped elicit a more candid answer.
wrongPassages: Police seized the elicit shipment before it crossed the border.
Quants discarded the elicit factor that explained most of the variance.
The held fifth was elicit under a modulation that never returned.
